guide.title: Kensington, Brooklyn: Ocean Parkway and Little Bangladesh
guide.intro: The land Kensington occupies was first colonised by Dutch farmers in the seventeenth century, inside the town of Flatbush, and re-settled by British colonists in 1737. Building began in 1885, after Ocean Parkway was completed, and the area took its name from the London borough at the turn of the twentieth century. Jeremiah Johnson Jr., president of the Brooklyn Real Estate Exchange, developed Kensington Heights around 1891 and Kensington-in-Flatbush around 1894; the town of Flatbush, the Kensington tracts included, was annexed by the City of Brooklyn in 1894, ahead of the consolidation of the five boroughs on January 1, 1898. For most of the twentieth century nobody called it Kensington at all. Residents, demographers and the press treated it as the western section of Flatbush, or West Flatbush, and the current name only took hold in the 1980s.

sections.heading: How Kensington got its name back
sections.body:
Rezoning during construction of the IND Culver subway line reshaped the housing stock. Six-storey elevator apartment buildings became increasingly common on upper Ocean Parkway and its side streets between the late 1920s and 1941, replacing many of the earlier suburban villas. After the Second World War, construction of the Prospect Expressway was followed by more apartment-house building on and near Ocean Parkway, including the Marlene J., later Caton Towers, and the Americana Towers, continuing to the mid-1960s. The Church Avenue streetcar line closed in 1956 and was replaced by buses.

The name came back administratively before it came back in speech. The city's 1969 Plan for New York City informally designated the tracts between McDonald and Coney Island Avenues as Kensington. Community boards had been established in 1963, and most of present-day Kensington had gone into the Borough Park-dominated Brooklyn Community Board 12 while eastern Flatbush and Midwood went into Community Board 14 — a split Wikipedia describes as possibly stemming from the Kensington Democratic leader Howard Golden's ties to Borough Park's Roosevelt Club. By the early 1980s, as the older Irish- and then Italian-American population aged out, real-estate interests adopted the Kensington name quickly, and the neighborhood drew young professionals, Orthodox Jews and immigrant communities during the city's co-op conversion movement.

Neighborhood boundaries here are contested and have never been officially defined by the city. A 2001 New York Times article gave Kensington's borders as Caton Avenue and Fort Hamilton Parkway on the north, 36th Street, Dahill Avenue and 47th Street on the west, Foster Avenue on the south and Coney Island Avenue on the east. The Encyclopedia of New York City in 2010 instead put the western edge at McDonald Avenue and carried the southern edge to Avenue H. The two do not agree, and neither is definitive.

sections.heading: Little Bangladesh
sections.body:
On October 16, 2022, City Council Member Shahana Hanif co-named the intersection of McDonald and Church Avenues Little Bangladesh. Hanif is the first Muslim woman elected to the New York City Council, a lifelong Kensington resident and the daughter of Bangladeshi immigrants. The co-naming recognises a corridor that is home to roughly 35 percent of the Bangladeshis living in New York City, most of them from the Chittagong, Sandwip and Noakhali regions, who began settling there in the early 1980s.

The corridor's food is the most visible part of it. Radhuni Sweets + Restaurant sits on McDonald Avenue just off Church Avenue, and Abdullah Sweets is on Church Avenue itself. A block away at McDonald Avenue and Avenue C, residents pushed to turn a long-unused vacant lot into a public plaza.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The IND Culver Line runs through the neighborhood. Church Avenue, an underground station at Church and McDonald Avenues in Kensington, is served by the F at all times and by the G at all times as the G's southern terminus, with limited peak-direction F express service. Fort Hamilton Parkway, also underground and served by the F and G at all times, sits on the Kensington and Windsor Terrace border.

South of there the line rises. Ditmas Avenue, an elevated station on the Kensington and Borough Park border, is served only by the F at all times and by peak-direction express trains; the G does not stop there. 18th Avenue, also elevated and also F-only, sits at the point where Borough Park, Kensington and Mapleton meet.

faq.question: How do I get to Kensington?
faq.answer: By subway on the IND Culver Line. Church Avenue at Church and McDonald Avenues is served by the F and by the G, which terminates there. Fort Hamilton Parkway, on the Kensington and Windsor Terrace border, is served by the F and G. Ditmas Avenue and 18th Avenue further south are F-only elevated stations.

faq.question: Why is Kensington sometimes called West Flatbush?
faq.answer: Because that is what it was called. For much of the twentieth century the area was seldom distinguished as its own neighborhood, and residents, demographers and the press identified it as the western section of Flatbush. The name Kensington, taken from the London borough at the turn of the twentieth century, was only adopted widely by real-estate interests in the early 1980s.

faq.question: What is Little Bangladesh?
faq.answer: A corridor around McDonald and Church Avenues, co-named on October 16, 2022 by Council Member Shahana Hanif. Roughly 35 percent of the Bangladeshis living in New York City live in the area, most from the Chittagong, Sandwip and Noakhali regions, and settlement there began in the early 1980s.

faq.question: Can I go inside the synagogues on the National Register?
faq.answer: Congregation Chevra Linath Hazedeck at 109 Clara Street and the Ocean Parkway Jewish Center at 550 Ocean Parkway are both listed on the National Register. No source consulted for this guide confirms whether non-congregants can visit the interiors, so treat them as buildings to look at from the street.

faq.question: Are there hotels in Kensington?
faq.answer: No lodging is listed here, and none is borrowed from a neighbouring neighborhood.

photos.title: The Kensington post office on McDonald Avenue
photos.description: A two-storey brick building with stone trim and a pedimented doorway, flags overhead and blue collection boxes on the pavement.
photos.author: Jim.henderson

photos.title: The Kensington branch library
photos.description: An orange-panelled library with a tall glazed bay, its Brooklyn Public Library sign facing the street between parked cars.
photos.author: Ehblake

places.name: Ocean Parkway
places.address: From Church Avenue to Seabreeze Avenue, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A boulevard designed by Olmsted and Vaux, between Church Avenue and Seabreeze Avenue. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on September 8, 1983, reference number 83001697.

places.name: United States Post Office, Kensington Station
places.summary: A post office building individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places on November 17, 1988, reference number 88002461, as part of the multiple-property submission US Post Offices in New York State, 1858-1943.
places.history: Its current use as an active retail post office is not confirmed by any citable source, so only the National Register listing is stated here.

places.name: Congregation Chevra Linath Hazedeck
places.summary: A synagogue, also known as the Kensington Synagogue, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on February 16, 2016, reference number 16000016. No source consulted confirms whether the interior is open to visitors.

places.name: Ocean Parkway Jewish Center
places.summary: A synagogue on Ocean Parkway listed on the National Register of Historic Places on December 11, 2009, reference number 09001082. No source consulted confirms whether the interior is open to visitors.

places.name: Dome Playground
places.address: 384 Dahill Road, between 37th and 38th Streets, Brooklyn, NY 11218
places.summary: A 1.385-acre NYC Parks playground on Dahill Road between 37th and 38th Streets, in zip code 11218. The city's parks-properties record lists it as an active property under Brooklyn Community Board 12.

places.name: Avenue C Plaza
places.address: McDonald Avenue at Avenue C, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A public plaza made from a long-unused vacant lot that residents pushed to reclaim. Council Member Shahana Hanif described it in 2022 as having hosted art installations, Ramadan iftar dinners and Dia de los Muertos observances. It is not a registered NYC Parks property.

places.name: Radhuni Sweets + Restaurant
places.summary: A Bangladeshi restaurant on McDonald Avenue just off Church Avenue, in the corridor co-named Little Bangladesh. City restaurant-inspection records list it at this address with an inspection dated January 7, 2026.

places.name: Abdullah Sweets
places.summary: A Bangladeshi sweets shop in the Little Bangladesh corridor. City restaurant-inspection data lists it at this address as an active establishment.
